The main weather event occurred on the 10th when tornadoes and swaths of intense straight-line winds ravaged the Tallahassee area. A severe squall line plowed through parts of SE AL, the FL Panhandle and Big Bend early that morning and produced a total of 7 confirmed tornadoes. Three tornadoes went through Leon County, of which two, each rated EF-2 (max winds of 115 mph), simultaneously converged on Tallahassee. That same storm also was responsible for destructive wind damage in excess of 100 mph with the FAMU Weatherstem site reporting a peak gust of 84 mph, while the Tallahassee Airport gusted to 66 mph. costliest.narrative: A persistent rainy pattern across southeastern Taylor county brought rainfall amounts in excess of foot during the first 12 days of the month. This rainfall fell on already saturated grounds and resulted in significant, long duration areal flooding. In addition, significant river flooding occurred across the Steinhatchee River basin.  The Steinhatchee River crested at its 2nd highest crest on record at 24.6 ft on August 7th, which is well into the moderate flood category.  Many roads were closed, and many homes were impacted.  The river remained in at least minor flood stage for 20 days.  Damage cost was estimated.

A tornado touched down briefly in downtown Perry, FL and was on the ground for about a minute. The tornado touched down west of South Quincy St. near W. Homer J. Smith Ave. It blew over a fence and pealed back a tin roof at a tavern. It continued east northeast along E. Hampton Springs Rd pulling up a carport cover that was anchored to the ground. The tornado bent over a stop sign and snapped large branches off a tree near the intersection of S. Jefferson St. and W. Hampton Springs Rd. One of these was hurled across the intersection, breaking a window of a home. The tornado then broke or bent several large tree limbs before damaging a fence east of Orange St. The tornado lifted just east of S. Center St.  This tornado was rated EF0 with max winds around 75 mph.

A tornado touched down south of Perry, FL on the north side of Houck Rd. Here the tornado produced EF-0 damage to a large metal building system, pulling some of the metal roof panels off the building and sending insulation over to Perry Foley Airport. Traveling southeast across Houck Rd, EF-1 damage was observed as the tornado then flipped up the metal roof of a porch, peeled back the metal roof of an outbuilding, snapped a tree and uprooted a very large tree. Further southeast at the airport a sign was damaged, debris from the metal building was found, and one aircraft broke free of its tail rope and was pushed sideways. The tornado then lifted shortly past the airport. Damage cost was estimated.
A storm survey indicated that straight line winds of 80 to 90 mph resulted in snapped trees, a destroyed shed, and roof damage in an area east of Perry along San Pedro Road.

recent.narrative: Northwest Florida started December with drought conditions ranging from D2-D4 across the area. Beneficial rain fell during the middle of the month, and the drought eased back to as low as D1 across some areas of the panhandle and southeast big bend by December 16th.

November started with D2 to D3 drought conditions across most of northwest Florida. By the end of the month, continued below average rainfall worsened conditions to D4 across portions of Jackson, Calhoun, Liberty, Gadsden, Leon, Wakulla, Jefferson, and Madison counties.

D2 drought conditions expanded across a larger area of the Florida panhandle and big bend by the middle of October. By the end of the month, the drought had worsened to D3 across portions of the inland Florida panhandle and big bend.
Dangerously cold wind chills of 10-15 degrees occurred.
In general, between 3 and 5 inches of snow fell across the county.
Very strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts of 50-60 mph well ahead of a squall line impacted coastal areas of the Florida panhandle eastward to coastal Wakulla county with downed trees and power lines.

costliest.narrative: In general, between 3 and 5 inches of snow fell across the county.
Several trees and power lines were blown down.

The coldest temperatures in about 10 years descended into the tri-state region during the Dec 24-26 period. Low temperatures dipped well down into the teens with high temperatures remaining in the 30s, and even at or below freezing in southeast Alabama on Dec 24th. This extended period of below freezing temperatures with hard freeze conditions resulted in numerous reports of broken pipes, primarily in northwest Florida. However, a few reports of broken pipes were also received from Cottonwood in Houston county. In addition, two homeless men were found dead from hypothermia after sleeping outside. One was in Wakulla county, and the other was in Leon county. Monetary damage from the broken pipes was estimated.
Very strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts of 50-60 mph well ahead of a squall line impacted coastal areas of the Florida panhandle eastward to coastal Wakulla county with downed trees and power lines.

recent.narrative: Continuation of the tornado track that originated in Hardee County after a long-lived supercell embedded within an outer rainband associated with Tropical Storm Debby tracked north-northwestward across much of interior southwest Florida, including parts of Lee, Charlotte and DeSoto counties, before a tornado was spotted west of Bowling Green and reported via a picture submitted by a NWS volunteer, around 12:25 EST. The tornado crossed into Polk County at 12:26 EST before it was estimated to have dissipated shortly thereafter north of County Line Rd, after traversing a mostly rural area. Maximum winds were estimated around 75 mph.

A supercell embedded within an outer rainband associated with Tropical Storm Debby began showing signs of increased organization around 13:40 EST as it moved north-northwest across southern Polk County between Bowling Green and Fort Meade. The storm continued exhibiting signs of increasing organization as it passed west of Fort Meade, before a NWS volunteer relayed video of a tornado associated with the storm around 13:58 EST just north of FL Hwy 640 near Agricola Rd. The volunteer relayed that the tornado continued on the ground for approximately 2 minutes before dissipating over open field after tracking around a mile and a half. No significant damage was reported, with likely only minor tree damage resulting from the tornado. Maximum winds were estimated around 75 mph.

Broadcast media shared video from a social media account depicting a very brief land spout tornado impacting a trailer and small carport-style structure, causing minor damage. No additional damage was reported.
Public video and reports shared via social media depict multiple fences toppled and damage to multiple pool cages just south of Lakeland Linder International Airport.
Picture posted on social media displayed golf ball size hail near Haines City.
Picture posted on social media displayed golf ball size hail near Lake Alfred.

Primary damage was near beginning of track where a home suffered roof damage. Elsewhere, most damage consisted of snapped or uprooted trees as the tornado tracked mostly over forested area.

Hernando County Sheriff's Office posted a video on social media detailing damage to a gas station in Spring Hill. Time estimated from radar.

FDEM relayed report from Pinellas County 911 dispatch of an individual injured by a lightning strike near Lealman, requiring transport for treatment following initial on-scene attention from local EMS and fire department personnel.

Tornadic waterspout came ashore, becoming a tornado near northern Clearwater Beach and continued across the Dunedin Channel before again coming ashore near Dunedin, near the intersection of the Dunedin Causeway and Hwy 19. Multiple homes in Clearwater Beach and Dunedin suffered at least minor roof damage, with a multi-story condominium building in Dunedin losing over a third of its roof along with part of the side wall, which was tossed about 500 yards away. A nearby strip mall also experienced partial roof loss and ensuing water damage, with a few damaged or destroyed concrete poles in its parking lot. Additionally, at least 3 other homes received mainly roof damage before the tornado dissipated just east of U.S. Hwy 19.

Strong thunderstorms developed over Pinellas County as the east and west coast sea breeze boundaries collided. A landspout tornado developed in Largo, FL, along colliding sea breeze and outflow boundaries.||The setup leading to the landspout's development was complex. Two boundaries collided over Largo - one from a strong cell to the southwest and one from another strong cell to the east. As these boundaries collided, a new updraft began to develop where the collision took place. Strong downdrafts from both cells essentially sandwiched the boundary and the developing updraft between the more mature cells - forcing the developing cell to take a deviant track to the north, right along the boundary collision. Volusia County Emergency Management reported limited damage across the county, mainly in the form of fallen trees and power lines. Surface observations indicate peak wind gusts generally between 45 to 55 mph. Rainfall totals ranged between 0.5 to 1.5 inches.

Hurricane Idalia's landfall along the Big Bend region led to widespread tropical storm force wind gusts through the day. The peak wind gust was 31 knots at the Deland Municipal Airport. No damage was reported.

Hurricane Nicole's extensive wind field led to a period of tropical storm force winds and heavy rain in Volusia County. Scattered reports of trees downed and some minor structural damage due to strong winds, which surface observations indicated peaked between 60 and 70 mph along the coast, and 45 to 55 mph across inland areas. No storm-related fatalities were reported by county officials.

Hurricane Ian's slow movement and large wind field led to a long period of tropical storm force winds in Volusia County. Scattered reports of trees and power lines downed, as well as generally minor damage to roofs, awnings, fences, and pool enclosures due to strong winds, which surface observations indicated peaked between 60 and 70 mph across inland areas.

The RAWS stations at Lake George, LGRF1, and Lake Woodruff, LWQF1, both measured a peak heat index of 115F. The Florida FAWN at Pierson, EPRF1, measured a peak heat index value of 122F. This occurred because west winds brought very moist air off of Lake George causing dew points at the Pierson FAWN to reach up to 83F.

costliest.narrative: Strong wind lasting for approximately three hours occurred in Volusia County, with peak observed wind gusts up to 48 mph. A trained spotter reported a large tree was downed in Port Orange, near Clyde Morris Boulevard and Colony Road.

A EF-1 tornado with maximum estimated winds of 90 mph tracked across The Eagles Golf Club northwest of Westchase, from just west of Birkdale Drive, across Nine Eagles Drive, Byrnwyck Lane and Benty Way, before lifting just west of Eagle Oak Drive. The most notable structural damage observed was the detachment/collapse of several pool cages backing up to the golf course. Additional roof and tree damage was noted, however, this appeared to be associated with inflow and/or an eventual microburst with a uniform direction to the damage. Along the path, there were a couple pockets of EF-1 damage. However, most of the surveyed damage was EF-0.

The tornado continued into St. Lucie County very near the intersection of the County Line Canal and Interstate 95 (near Mile Marker 114).

Behind the convenience store, a house was heavily damaged with portions of the roof missing, but most of the damage to this home came from the roof of the store landing on it. recent.narrative: Coastal flooding occurred along the Brevard County coast after strong northeast winds and large breaking surf persisted for seven consecutive high tide cycles from November 6-9. The strong winds occurred in conjunction with the highest astronomical tides of the year, with the greatest total water levels observed on November 7-8. At Trident Pier (TRDF1), the highest observed water level was 2.76 FT MHHW on November 7th, and a secondary peak of 2.61 FT MHHW was observed on November 8th. Brevard County Emergency Management and local beach patrol reported minor to moderate beach erosion, and water approaching a few coastal roads due to water backing up from the Indian River. Significant water run-up occurred toward the dunes at many county beaches.

A 69-year-old white male from Oregon was swimming in the surf around 1630LST off Jerry Park in Cape Canaveral (an unguarded beach) when family members lost sight of him. He was then located unresponsive in the water approximately 100 yards offshore and transported to a local hospital in critical condition where he was later pronounced deceased. Although no one saw what actually happened, his family reported feeling a strong current pulling away from shore. He was considered a strong swimmer that had visited many beaches before. Distant Hurricane Larry produced moderate, long-period swells on this day, leading to a high risk of numerous and strong rip currents. The Medical Examiner listed drowning as the cause of death.

Waterspout. Location: 28.5412N, 80.9397W. An isolated thunderstorm developed and slowly moved south across northern Brevard county. A photo posted on social media confirmed that this storm produced a brief waterspout on the St. Johns River near the State Road 50 boat ramp, just east of the town of Christmas.

Two local residents were swimming together at Juan Ponce de Leon Landing Beach in Melbourne Beach when they became trapped in a rip current. The first victim was a 23-year-old female who was unable to be revived at a local hospital. The second victim was a 26-year-old male who disappeared beneath the water. His body was recovered the following afternoon a few miles to the north of where he went missing.

A group of tourists from Indiana were visiting Cocoa Beach. A 45-year-old man attempted to aid a female member of his group who was struggling to swim after being caught in a rip current. Cocoa Beach Fire Department personnel deployed a jet ski, and the man and woman were brought to shore. The man was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The female was treated, and she survived.

A 50-year old man from Michigan went missing after being caught in a rip current and rough surf while swimming near Cherie Down Park in Cape Canaveral. The search was called off the following day and man was presumed drowned. Near the time the man went missing, his nephew was rescued from the water by a surfer.

costliest.narrative: The 344 Wildfire burned over 20,000 acres in extreme southeast Miami-Dade County, ignited near East Palm Drive and SW 117th Ave, near Homestead. On March 13th, it was reported to be approximately 700 acres and 50 percent contained. No injuries, evacuations, or endangerments were reported at the time. With a strong easterly wind and gusts up to 25 mph, containment was lost and the fire began to rapidly grow on March 18th. Smoke covered the roadways of US-1 and Card Sound Roads. US 1 and Card Sound roads were closed between Florida City and Key Largo intermittingly for several days preventing access to and from mainland Florida and the Keys. Miami-Dade EM reported several power lines on Card Sound Road had been burned down and damage to several communication towers. By the end of March, the Florida Forest Service reported that the 344 Wildfire was at 26,719 acres and 85 percent containment

The Florida Forest Service reported that the 344 Wildfire, in extreme Southeast Miami-Dade County, had burned a total 26,719 acres. As of April 4th, the wildfire was 100 percent contained. No injuries or fatalities were reported. There was damage to power lines and communication towers, but no significant damage from the fire.

Several downed trees were reported across areas of coastal Miami-Dade County early on the morning of November 16th due to frequent wind gusts up to 65 mph as a wake low moved across the area. Thousands of people in the area were left without power as trees fell on power lines. Extensive tree damage was observed in the Miami Beach area, with a few uprooted trees and large tree branches falling onto roofs, vehicles, and power lines. Wind gusts were measured by several ASOS and mesonet stations.

recent.narrative: Hurricane Rafael produced a period of tropical storm force winds primarily across the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County.  Sustained winds of 25 to 35 mph with peak wind gusts of 40 to 55 mph occurred, downing a few small tree limbs.  No significant power outages were reported.  Peak wind gusts were measured at 39 mph with a gust to 53 mph at the Naval Air Station Key West Boca Chica Field, and 36 mph with a gust to 47 mph at Key West International Airport.

Minor coastal flooding along the Atlantic-side facing coast of Key West, Stock Island, and Boca Chica Key occurred as a combination of water levels reaching near 1.2 feet above mean higher high water (MHHW) and wave overwash.  Minor street flooding occurred along with a temporary closure of State Road A1A (South Roosevelt Boulevard) in Key West within an ongoing construction zone.

Tropical storm conditions overspread the Lower Florida Keys and Key West as the result of the passage of Hurricane Milton well to the north of the Florida Keys.  Frequent wind gusts of 45 to 60 mph impacted the Lower Florida Keys, with the maximum sustained winds near 40 mph with gusts to 59 mph observed at Key West International Airport.  Scattered, mostly small power outages occurred as result of downed tree limbs, with the largest power outage impacting a portion of east-central Big Pine Key at over 100 customers.

Coastal flooding was initially limited to street flooding and heavy wave overwash of seawalls on the Atlantic side of Key West, and later evolved on the Gulf of Mexico side of the Lower Keys.  Maximum water levels were measured at 1.2 feet above MHHW in the protected Key West Harbor, but estimated at 2.0 to 2.5 feet above MHHW along the northern extends of Big Torch Key and Big Pine Key.

Minor oceanside flooding occurred in Key West as result of storm surge flooding and heavy wave action, requiring temporary closer of a construction zone on State Road A1A.  Minor flooding of 6 to 18 inches depth occurred on other exposed oceanside streets in southwest Key West.

Wind Impacts in the Florida Keys of Monroe County consisted of several rain bands and gradient winds of lower tropical-storm force.  Sustained winds in the 25 to 40 mph range with frequent gusts of 45 to 55 mph were most prevalent across the far western Lower Florida Keys and the City of Key West.  Sporadic, short-duration power outages occurred with the largest outages affecting approximately 850 customers on Stock Island during the early morning of September 27th.  Several instances of large tree limbs were downed mainly in the Lower Florida Keys along with a couple trees, with resulting utility line damage.

costliest.narrative: Tropical Storm-force wind impacts occurred mainly with a single rain band that passed through the Lower Florida Keys during the late morning and early afternoon hours of August 29, 2023. A couple large royal poinciana trees were felled in Key West, with one damaging a vehicle.   Maximum sustained winds of 44 knots with a gust to 55 knots was measured at an electrical substation on Big Coppitt Key, with sustained winds of 39 knots with gusts to 51 knots measured by the ASOS at the Naval Air Station Key West Boca Chica Airfield.

Low temperatures dipped well down into the teens with high temperatures remaining in the 30s, and even at or below freezing in southeast Alabama on Dec 24th. This extended period of below freezing temperatures with hard freeze conditions resulted in numerous reports of broken pipes, primarily in northwest Florida. However, a few reports of broken pipes were also received from Cottonwood in Houston county. In addition, two homeless men were found dead from hypothermia after sleeping outside. One was in Wakulla county, and the other was in Leon county. Monetary damage from the broken pipes was estimated.

November started with D2 to D3 drought conditions across most of northwest Florida. By the end of the month, continued below average rainfall worsened conditions to D4 across portions of Jackson, Calhoun, Liberty, Gadsden, Leon, Wakulla, Jefferson, and Madison counties.
